note: Shot-by-shot teardowns for study. Prompt reconstructions are analytical reconstructions for teaching, NOT the productions' actual prompts. Every production fact carries its research source.

teardowns.context: Girl realizes pre-flight that her passport is across town and races through an absurd apocalypse to get it back. Pipeline: hand-drawn storyboards → character design in Soul 2.0 → hand-painted Photoshop refinements → Blender previs → structured video prompts → Seedance 2.5 generation. The whole production was released open — every storyboard, every Blender scene, every prompt.

shots.breaks: Nothing broke here; this is the stage that prevented breaks later.
shots.lesson: Storyboard everything, even if you can't draw. Boards are the cheapest generation you'll ever make — a bad board costs minutes, a bad generation costs credits.
shots.setup: Hand-drawn storyboards locked the story before a single generation was bought. Per third-party commentary on the production: what the client approved in the boards is what ends up on screen.
shots.title: The boards before the budget
shots.works: Story decisions were made at the cheapest possible stage — pencil, not credits. 18 car-chase scenes were boarded before production started.

shots.breaks: Where previs was thin, generations drifted — unmotivated camera movement is one of the documented failure modes.
shots.lesson: Previs is the camera department. Decide the move, the timing, and the action beat in a free tool before spending credits.
shots.prompt_reconstruction: Reconstruction for study, not the actual prompt — "Watercolor-stylized 3D girl sprints left-to-right across frame, camera tracks laterally at her pace, squash-and-stretch on each stride, motion-blurred background, one continuous move, no camera shake."
shots.setup: Blender was used for camera movement, action timing, and squash-and-stretch — the motion was decided in previs, then AI animation executed it.
shots.title: Blender previs as the camera department
shots.works: One motivated camera move per shot, timed in previs. The AI model never had to invent motion grammar; it only had to execute it.

shots.breaks: Subtle acting collapses: micro-expressions either freeze or overshoot into caricature. The model can do broad action; it cannot do a held-back feeling without direction.
shots.lesson: Direct tactics, not emotions. 'She decides not to cry' beats 'she looks sad' — a playable action gives the model something physical to do. See the directing-performance chapter.
shots.prompt_reconstruction: Reconstruction for study, not the actual prompt — weak version: 'girl looks sad in taxi, cinematic.' Directed version: 'girl stares out taxi window, decides not to cry, jaw tightens once, looks down at her hands, holds still. Camera: slow push-in, stop on her eyes.'
shots.setup: The production's own breakdown dedicates a section to 'why AI struggles with subtle character acting' and 'three challenging shots' — quiet reaction beats where the character had to feel something small.
shots.title: The subtle-acting shots (the hard ones)
shots.works: The team identified the failure honestly instead of cutting around it — naming the weakness is what made the breakdown valuable.

shots.breaks: Early tests show missing character details — the failures the breakdown honestly includes. Reference gaps = drift.
shots.lesson: Every shot gets its reference. Character sheets, approved stills, locked start frames: consistency is a supply chain, not a prompt trick.
shots.setup: The team kept camera angles and character details consistent across 18 scenes produced in three days, using 'carefully prepared image references' to bring stylized 3D characters into a watercolor world.
shots.title: Consistency discipline across 18 scenes in 3 days
shots.works: Image references did the consistency work — the video model was never asked to remember what a character looked like; it was shown, every shot.

shots.breaks: Lighting tests that failed, characters that lost details — each one is a labeled failure mode with a visible fix.
shots.lesson: Budget for design tests and keep your failures. A production that documents what broke is worth more than a showreel that hides it. This guide's failure-gallery chapter works the same way.
shots.setup: The official breakdown shows failed generations, missing character details, and lighting tests — the production published its mistakes alongside its wins.
shots.title: The failure reel
shots.works: The failure reel is the most instructive part of the release: it shows exactly where the pipeline's guardrails are.

teardowns.subtitle: Hybrid AI animation · Higgsfield Originals (2026)
teardowns.title: Passport Rush

teardowns.context: Four friends in a dorm; three imagined worlds (a Troy battle, a galactic cruiser chase, a griffin flight over a fairytale valley). ~41,118 assets for ~20 minutes. The production brief was open-sourced (via community transcription — flagged as third-party of a first-party brief). Note: ONEIRIC has no verified Cannes premiere; the Cannes-adjacent screening was for Hell Grind, a separate work.

shots.breaks: Without the diagram, eyelines and positions drifted shot to shot — the classic multi-character failure.
shots.lesson: Block dialogue like a stage play before you generate. A simple color-coded map beats a paragraph of spatial description in every prompt.
shots.prompt_reconstruction: Reconstruction for study, not the actual prompt — 'Diagram: blue = Rudy seated left on couch, green = Mara standing right by window. Shot: MCU on the blue, Rudy looks up at the green (eyeline upper-right of frame), says his line, holds. Do not move either character's seat position.'
shots.setup: One-room dialogue continuity was 'the hardest technical task of the film — harder than the space battle.' Four characters talking in one room for minutes, without morphing.
shots.title: The living-room dialogue (the hardest shot in the film)
shots.works: The color-coded Diagram Skill: a schematic outline drawing attached as reference alongside real refs, each color bound to a character tag ('MCU on the blue', 'POV of the green'). Coverage became conversational.

shots.breaks: Lens descriptions in video prompts decayed within a scene; every shot needed re-anchoring.
shots.lesson: Put what the model drops into the asset, not the prompt. The image stage is where look is locked; the video stage is where motion happens.
shots.prompt_reconstruction: Reconstruction for study, not the actual prompt — image-stage: 'Living room, STRONG anamorphic look baked in: horizontal squeeze, oval elliptical bokeh in background lamps, stretched window highlights, subtle barrel edge distortion, chromatic aberration on high-contrast edges. NO lens flares. 2.39:1.' Video-stage: 'Match the reference image exactly; only animate: dust in the light beam, curtain sway.'
shots.setup: Asking the video model for 'anamorphic' produced optics that drifted shot to shot. The fix: generate the location IMAGE with anamorphic already baked in — horizontal squeeze, oval bokeh, stretched highlights — and let the video model read the optics off the asset.
shots.title: The consistent-lens-look trick
shots.works: 'The plate itself becomes the lens.' Lens, grade, texture, time of day — anything the video model kept dropping — moved into the image asset, not the video prompt.

shots.breaks: Earlier text-only chaining accumulated drift: wardrobe, lighting, and faces slowly migrated scene to scene.
shots.lesson: Chain finished pixels, not descriptions. The last approved frame is the best prompt for the next shot.
shots.setup: Each new scene was generated with the previous scene's FINISHED VIDEO as reference — not a text description of it.
shots.title: The carried-reference chain
shots.works: 'A text description drifts over generations — a video reference doesn't.' The chain held look and identity across 20 minutes.

shots.breaks: Emotion-word prompts produced the dead-glassy-eyes failure — mathematical stillness where micro-movement should be.
shots.lesson: Direct the eyes like blocking, not like mood. Every pair of eyes gets a job per beat. See the dead-eyes checklist.
shots.prompt_reconstruction: Reconstruction for study, not the actual prompt — weak: 'she looks sad, cinematic close-up.' Directed: 'Close-up: she hears the news, eyes drop to the table (beat), then lift to his face and hold — do not blink for the first two seconds. Micro-asymmetry, natural skin texture.'
shots.setup: The acting system banned emotion words: 'Write sad and you get a caricature or a dead face.' Instead, eye-work was named as action — a named eyeline, a glance with a target.
shots.title: Giving the eyes a job
shots.works: Named eye actions (look away on the beat, hold the gaze through the line) produced the shots that read as thinking instead of posing.

shots.breaks: Continuous re-rolling burned credits and produced 'almost' takes that were never approved.
shots.lesson: Approve, then photograph. The instruction after approval changes from 'generate this scene' to 'photograph this exact performance from a new angle.'
shots.setup: Generation supervision happened as a scheduled pass after the rough cut — QC plus re-generation of broken shots — not as continuous re-rolling. Once a take was approved, it was locked: re-render the camera around it, never regenerate the performance.
shots.title: Scene Lock and scheduled regeneration
shots.works: Iteration became a department with a calendar instead of a standing reaction. Version logs recorded version, what changed, verdict.

teardowns.subtitle: 20-minute photoreal drama · Higgsfield / Cinema Studio 4 (2026)
teardowns.title: ONEIRIC

teardowns.context: A 5-minute film on the Phaeacians and Princess Nausicaa, made with Grok Imagine, won a $100,000 grand prize — then was panned in the press for visual inconsistencies. The coverage framed it as highlighting 'the current limitations of AI filmmaking, even with a substantial prize at stake.' The lesson the guide takes: a prize does not forgive broken continuity.

shots.breaks: No identity lock on the creature design: the model's averaging produced an extra eye. No QC pass caught it before delivery.
shots.lesson: Consistency is the floor. A locked character sheet, checked against every generation, would have caught this in minutes. Polish is not optional at any budget — the press will find the third eye.
shots.setup: The film's Cyclops appears with three eyes — a character-design failure visible to every viewer, in the winning film of a six-figure contest.
shots.title: The three-eyed Cyclops
shots.works: The spectacle and ambition were real — epic scale is what the contest rewarded.

shots.breaks: No exclusion block ('deformed hands, extra limbs, melting anatomy'), no hands discipline, no post crop pass.
shots.lesson: Put anatomy guards in every prompt, not just the risky ones — and check the edges of frame, not just the hero. See the prompt-engineering exclusion block.
shots.setup: Background and mid-ground characters render with feet instead of hands — the classic anatomy failure, shipped in a prize-winning film.
shots.title: Feet for hands
shots.works: Foreground hero shots held together; the failure is in the unguarded edges of frame.

shots.breaks: Decoupled dialogue: lines generated without native-audio planning, without attributed delivery, without performance arcs — the voice carries nothing because nothing was directed.
shots.lesson: Dialogue is a department, not a checkbox. Attribute every line, direct delivery through the text, or plan the edit around native audio. See the directing-performance chapter.
shots.setup: The dialogue was singled out as awkward — the film's weakest non-visual element.
shots.title: The awkward dialogue
shots.works: The story ambition (a full Odyssey episode in 5 minutes) is genuine.

teardowns.subtitle: Artist-led AI animation · Google DeepMind (2026)
teardowns.context: Six-minute animated short directed by Pixar alum Connie He, premiered at the Sundance Film Festival in January 2026. A 45-person crew of animators and Google DeepMind researchers built the film around custom fine-tuned Veo and Imagen models trained on production designer Yingzong Xin's artwork. Rough animation was made first in the animators' own tools (Maya, TVPaint) and transformed into the final expressionist style via video-to-video; no final shot was a one-click generation. Dailies, localized refinement tools, and a Veo 4K upscale finished the pipeline.

shots.title: Rough animation first, AI second
shots.setup: Animators blocked every performance in their own tools — traditional 3D in Maya, hand-drawn 2D in TVPaint — before any AI touched a frame. Timing, comedic rhythm, and acting choices were made by humans with pencils and rigs, exactly as in a conventional production.
shots.works: The film's comedy lands because the timing was directed, not prompted. The AI's job was transformation — turning approved rough motion into the final painterly style — so human intention survived every shot.
shots.breaks: Early text-prompt-only attempts failed the film's core need: per third-party coverage of the production, characters moved in random, uncontrolled ways when driven by words alone. Text could not carry comedic timing, motion rhythm, or precise framing.
shots.lesson: Direct motion with drawings, not words. For performance-driven work, the prompt is the weakest control surface you have — rough animation is the strongest. AI works best here as a stylization layer, not an idea generator.

shots.title: Fine-tune on the production designer's art
shots.setup: Instead of prompting a general model toward a style, the team fine-tuned custom Veo and Imagen models on artwork made specifically for the film by production designer Yingzong Xin. A few example images taught the models new visual concepts.
shots.works: Consistency across shots — the historic failure point of AI animation. The models learned deep rules, not surface texture: Ada's hair silhouette never obscures her face (a 2D rule that violates 3D geometry), two-point perspective discipline, and the expressionist brushwork language.
shots.breaks: General-purpose models could not hold Ada's design rules; the character's look was too specific for a base model to reproduce reliably. Prompt adjectives ('expressionist', 'painterly') were not enough to lock it.
shots.lesson: Style-lock via training data beats style-lock via adjectives. When the dataset is yours, two hard problems get easier at once: visual consistency and clean authorship — the output inherits your rights position instead of the internet's.

shots.title: Video-to-video with an adjustable leash
shots.setup: The core technical workflow: rough animated sequences fed into the fine-tuned Veo models and transformed into fully stylized footage, with an adjustable balance between firm control and improvisation — inspired by how animators already communicate shot concepts by drawing or acting out scenes.
shots.works: Motion and timing intent survived the transformation while the frames gained the hand-painted finish. Animators could direct the AI the way they direct assistants: show the movement, set how much freedom it gets.
shots.breaks: A fixed control level would have failed both ends — too rigid kills the painterly life, too loose loses the performance. The production needed the dial, and had to build tooling to get it.
shots.lesson: Control versus improvisation is a dial, not a switch. When evaluating any video model, ask where the control dial lives — if the only settings are 'prompt harder' and 'regenerate', you don't have a production tool.

shots.title: Dailies, not one-click
shots.setup: Per the production accounts, none of the final shots were one-click generations. The team ran dailies, critiqued every shot through multiple feedback rounds, and built tools for localized refinement — fixing one region of a shot without regenerating the whole thing.
shots.works: Quality control scaled: a bad sleeve didn't cost a good face. Localized fixes kept iteration cheap and preserved approved work instead of gambling it on every regeneration.
shots.breaks: The fantasy that AI removes iteration. This production refutes it directly — the slow, repetitive, judgment-heavy part of filmmaking survived intact; only its shape changed.
shots.lesson: Keep the review discipline. AI changes what you iterate (regions and passes instead of frames and layers), not whether you iterate. Budget dailies into every AI production plan.

shots.title: Upscale as finish
shots.setup: Final shots were upscaled to 4K with Veo's upscaling, tuned to preserve the hand-painted aesthetic and rough expressionist brushwork rather than smoothing it into video-real detail.
shots.works: Theatrical resolution without losing the film's identity. The finish pipeline respected the style instead of fighting it — grain and brushwork survived the upscale.
shots.breaks: Generic upscalers would have 'cleaned' the very texture that made the film distinctive. Finish tools chosen without style-awareness destroy the look they are meant to enhance.
shots.lesson: The finish is part of the style system. Test your upscale/grade chain against your style bible's texture rules before committing — resolution means nothing if the look doesn't survive it.
